Even though there is no substantial evidence of confounding between patient characteristics and the use of delamanid (DLM), we will treat delamanid as a unique drug and adjust for its use in the multivariable analyses described below. This approach is similar to how we handle other drugs like linezolid (LZD) or later-generation fluoroquinolones (FQNs). Step 3: Analysis of the Duration of Bedaquiline (BDQ) To evaluate the potential benefits of extending bedaquiline treatment beyond 24 weeks, we plan to employ two analytical methods and compare their results. These analyses will be conducted for each of the four outcomes defined earlier, and sensitivity analyses will be performed for each method. Method 1: Exact and Propensity Score Matching Baseline patient characteristics with missing data will be imputed using multivariate imputation via chained equations. However, exposure and outcome data will not be imputed. Patients who received bedaquiline for 24 weeks will be matched to those who received it for a longer duration using a combination of exact matching and propensity score-based matching. This matching will account for covariates likely to influence treatment extension at week 24. The covariates include: Baseline characteristics: Resistance to fluoroquinolones (FQ) or second-line injectables (SLI), total number of drugs the patient is resistant to, acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear status, presence of cavitation on chest X-ray (CXR), HIV co-infection and antiretroviral therapy (ART) use, prior treatment history (first-line drugs only or also second-line drugs), age, and sex. During-treatment characteristics: Culture status at weeks 12 and 16 (conversion or non-conversion), number of acquired or new resistances at week 16 (0, 1, or 2+), cumulative number of drugs stopped due to adverse events by week 24 (0, 1, or 2+), radiologic findings at week 24, and treatment regimen at week 24, including the use of fluoroquinolones, linezolid, delamanid, and the number of other likely effective medications. We will attempt to match patients exactly on as many covariates as possible, recognizing that this may be challenging within the EndTB dataset. Propensity score matching will be applied to the remaining covariates. Covariates selected for exact matching will be those most strongly associated with the outcomes of interest. Propensity score matching will be applied to the remaining covariates. Additionally, we will consider clustering by site and further adjust for the year of treatment initiation and/or country-level income. Adjusted odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals will be estimated. For each analysis, the matched groups will be examined using standard reports to assess the improvement (or lack thereof) in the balance of characteristics between the two groups after applying the matching algorithm. Method 2: Survival Analysis Using Inverse Probability Weighting (IPTW) We will examine exposure in two ways: 1. Dichotomous: Patients who received only six months of bedaquiline versus those who received more than six months. 2. Continuous: Treating the duration of bedaquiline use beyond six months as a continuous variable. The primary outcome of interest will be a composite of failure, relapse, or death. Loss to follow-up (LTFU) will be treated as a censoring event. Patient time will be included until the end of follow-up for relapse. A baseline patient profile will be constructed based on clinical information available at month 6, including time-fixed covariates such as age, sex, and prior treatment history. Time-varying information, such as the receipt of concomitant drugs, number of adverse events requiring drug discontinuation, culture status, and radiologic findings, will be updated monthly. For patients stopping bedaquiline at month 6, IPTW will be estimated for all time points. For those continuing bedaquiline beyond month 6, IPTW will be estimated until the time of bedaquiline discontinuation, after which it will be considered constant. A survival analysis will then be conducted, clustering by patients and centers, and incorporating the calculated IPTW and IPCW weights. This analysis will be performed for both dichotomous and continuous outcomes. Question 2: Improved Treatment Outcomes with Extended Bedaquiline Use In the IPD-2019 dataset, we will assess whether treatment outcomes improve in patients who take bedaquiline for more than six months compared to those who take no bedaquiline or bedaquiline for six months. Exposure 1: No use of bedaquiline (<30 days). Reference (Comparator) 1: Use of bedaquiline for 24 weeks. Exposure 2: Use of bedaquiline for >24 weeks. We propose three analyses: 1. Comparing no bedaquiline to 24 weeks of bedaquiline. 2. Comparing 24 weeks of bedaquiline to >24 weeks of bedaquiline. 3. A combined analysis where bedaquiline use is treated as a three-level categorical variable (none, 24 weeks, and >24 weeks). Patients will be matched exactly on baseline characteristics such as fluoroquinolone and second-line injectable resistance, HIV co-infection and ART use, and country-level income. Further matching will be performed using propensity scores for age, sex, prior TB treatment, extent of disease (AFB smear and/or cavitation on CXR), use of linezolid, use of fluoroquinolones, use of delamanid, BMI (dichotomized as underweight or not), and the number of other effective drugs in the initial regimen. Due to limitations in detailed information about changes and events during therapy, these variables cannot be included in this analysis. Question 3: Combined IPD-2019 and EndTB Dataset Analysis We will assess whether treatment outcomes improve in patients who take bedaquiline for more than six months compared to those who take no bedaquiline or bedaquiline for six months. The exposure groups and comparators will be the same as in Question 2. The analytic approach will follow the same methodology as described in Question 2. Analysis of Adverse Events (AEs) The analysis of adverse events is complicated by uncertainties regarding the availability of data from the EndTB study. In the IPD-2019 dataset, we have information on the type of adverse events, the drug considered responsible, and whether the drug was permanently stopped. We propose three approaches to analyze the occurrence of adverse events: 1. Standard aggregate data meta-analysis for proportions. 2. Estimation of adverse event proportions for each drug using generalized linear mixed models with random effects at the cohort level. 3. Use of a multivariate Bayesian mixed model to estimate population-averaged treatment-specific event proportions. For each approach, we will assess the ranking of bedaquiline in terms of adverse event incidence among patients who received it for six months versus those who received it for longer durations. Changes in ranking would indicate differences in adverse event incidence between the groups. Limitations Patients receiving prolonged bedaquiline may have been sicker or had fewer treatment options, which could confound the analysis. However, differences in bedaquiline prescription and duration across countries and over time may create a quasi-experimental situation with less confounding due to patient characteristics. While we will use methods to control for confounding, unmeasured confounding cannot be completely eliminated. If unmeasured confounding is related to indication, it may underestimate the benefit of bedaquiline, as sicker patients or those with fewer effective drugs are more likely to receive prolonged bedaquiline. Potential Sensitivity Analyses 1. Accounting for missed doses due to non-adherence during the initial 24 weeks of bedaquiline exposure. 2. Assessing time to loss to follow-up, dropout, or default in patients taking no bedaquiline, six months of bedaquiline, and >6 months of bedaquiline. 3. Examining whether the effect of prolonged bedaquiline depends on other drugs used in the treatment regimen. 4. Analyzing the effect of bedaquiline prolongation in patients whose regimens would be compromised if bedaquiline were withdrawn. 5. Considering time non-linearly using splines or quadratic terms for duration. 6. Treating loss to follow-up as an outcome rather than a censoring event. 7. Comparing the frequency of specific drug-related adverse events in the EndTB and NixTB studies. Adverse events in the EndTB study are classified using severity grades 1–5 according to the MSF severity scale and standard criteria for serious events.
